column4: This ayah forbids both slaughter “عَلَى النُّصُبِ” and seeking shares “بِالْأَزْلَامِ”; it names the altar and arrow-allotment practices that the section reconstructs.
The section’s words al-maysir, al-anṣāb, and al-azlām appear together here as “رِجْسٌ مِّنْ عَمَلِ الشَّيْطَانِ,” giving the camel-and-stone scene its explicit Qur’anic judgment.
The section’s word al-maysir is the subject of this question; the answer says its sin is greater than its benefit, framing the game’s apparent gain as a loss.
This ayah describes a rite in which communities name Allah over the livestock He provides; it sets animal sacrifice directed to Allah against blood poured on worshipped stones.

For “الْبُدْنَ,” this ayah commands Allah’s name over the standing camels, then eating and feeding from them; it gives the section’s divided camel meat a sacrificial sharing ordered by God rather than arrows.
Following the camel rite of 22:36, this ayah says “لَن يَنَالَ اللَّهَ لُحُومُهَا وَلَا دِمَاؤُهَا” but that piety reaches Him; it overturns the section’s image of blood presented on a stone.
The command “فَصَلِّ لِرَبِّكَ وَانْحَرْ” directs prayer and slaughter to “your Lord,” matching the section’s conclusion that upright devotion faces the Lord rather than an altar stone.
The speaker declares “إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي” are for Allah, Lord of the worlds; this makes sacrifice and worship answer to God, not the section’s blood-marked stones.

The section’s dictionary word al-anṣāb names stones set up for worship; here people rush from graves “كَأَنَّهُمْ إِلَىٰ نُصُبٍ يُوفِضُونَ,” turning that stone image into an eschatological simile rather than a cultic rite.
The section’s root ش ر ح appears in Moses’s request “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي”; his plea for an opened chest before speaking gives another prophetic setting for the chest-opening named in 94:1.
The section’s root ش ر ح and word ṣadr recur in “يَشْرَحْ صَدْرَهُ لِلْإِسْلَامِ”; the same ayah contrasts that opening with a constricted chest, making the image a sign of guidance and its opposite.
The section’s root ش ر ح and word ṣadr recur when Allah opens a person’s chest to Islam; the ayah sets that opening against hearts hardened to God’s remembrance.
As the next ayah after 5:90, it names al-maysir’s effects: enmity and diversion from Allah’s remembrance and prayer. That consequence opposes the section’s movement toward the Lord.
The section’s dictionary form al-naṣīb means an appointed share; this verse calls an heir’s portion “نَصِيبًا مَفْرُوضًا,” placing allotment under a prescribed rule rather than arrow-lots.

The section’s dictionary word al-naṣīb means a set share; here “نَصِيبًا” is assigned from crops and livestock to Allah and partners, exposing rival cultic allocations beside the camel-and-stone scene.
This ayah says pens were cast as lots to choose who would care for Maryam; the lot action parallels the section’s arrows, while its own context shows selection for custodianship rather than gambling.
Jonah “فَسَاهَمَ” (cast lots) aboard the ship; the same lot-drawing action as the section’s meysir serves here to identify a passenger, not divide a gambling stake.

The section’s root ي س ر links its word yusr (ease) with al-maysir (gambling); here Allah intends “الْيُسْرَ” rather than “الْعُسْرَ” in the fasting rule, making ease a divine provision rather than chance gain.
The section’s root ي س ر also names its ease; this ayah promises “بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا” in its directions about spending, echoing ease with hardship and contrasting it with a share drawn by lot.
The section’s root ي س ر links al-maysir to ease; this ayah uses “مَيْسَرَةٍ” for a debtor’s time of ease, a merciful deferral that contrasts with gambling for a share.

The section’s root ي س ر links ease with al-maysir; after describing giving and God-consciousness, this ayah says “فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ,” an ethically directed ease rather than a chance allotment.

The section’s root ي س ر recurs in Allah’s address to the Prophet, “وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ”; ease is granted for his prophetic course, extending the surah’s promised ease beyond the gambling sense of al-maysir.

Immediately before 5:3, this ayah forbids violating Allah’s rites and the sacrificial offerings; it establishes protected, God-marked sacrifice before 5:3 distinguishes it from slaughter at the standing stones and allotment by arrows.

In the pilgrimage passage continued by 22:34 and 22:36, this ayah directs pilgrims to name Allah over the livestock He provided and to eat and feed the poor; its own contribution is a God-directed sharing of sacrificial meat, unlike the section’s arrow-divided camel.

This ayah in the same pilgrimage passage commands avoidance of the filth of idols; it directly marks the worship of standing stones as the rejected side of the legitimate rites described in 22:34 and 22:36.

This ayah says that honoring Allah’s signs is from piety of the hearts; beside 22:36, which calls sacrificial camels Allah’s signs, it distinguishes God-oriented rites from the section’s blood-offering to stones.

This ayah says the sacrificial animals’ destination is the Ancient House; alongside 22:34’s prescribed rite, its own detail gives a sanctuary-directed setting for animal sacrifice rather than the section’s erected altar stones.

The section’s dictionary form al-naṣīb is an appointed share; this ayah describes people assigning a portion of God’s provision to beings they do not know, showing how allotment of provision can serve a rival cult rather than a divinely prescribed share.

The section’s dictionary word al-naṣīb means a share; this ayah gives men and women a “نَصِيبٌ” from what they earn, grounding a person’s portion in accountable earning rather than the section’s chance-drawn stake.

Continuing the inheritance portions introduced at 4:7, this ayah sets out children’s and parents’ fractional shares as a rule; its own detail shows measured entitlement in place of arrows deciding who receives the camel meat.
This ayah continues the prescribed inheritance shares with fractions for spouses and siblings; its own allocation by kinship extends the contrast with the section’s chance-drawn portions.
This ayah assigns a fifth of war spoils to named recipients; the specified fraction and beneficiaries give a concrete case of a portion determined by rule rather than by the section’s arrows.
Abraham asks his people about “التَّمَاثِيلَ” to which they are devoted; these worshipped images parallel the section’s erected stones and make the object of devotion itself visible.
Abraham challenges worship of “مَا تَنْحِتُونَ,” what people carve; this parallels the section’s humanly erected and worshipped stones by confronting devotion to a made object.
